old: **Regarding the deities to whom this epithet applies: Nirukta scholars — Riśṭaṃ himsati** (i.e., "riśa" is destroyed [by the deity]); Riśaṃ hiṃsakaṃ dasyati (destroys the harmer); Riśam adyaṃ hiṃsanti dasyanti (destroy that which harms); **Riśam adyanti kṣipanti veti riśādasaḥ** — thus various authors explain it, some saying that they eat or consume the harmful, some that they hurl them away.** Devarājayajvan, in his commentary on the Nighaṇṭu (4-3-53), says the root *riś* is used in the sense of harming (Dhātupāṭha 33-72). **Vāyu and other deities' epithets are likewise described using the word "riśādasaḥ" in many places.**
new: **Mahīdhara, the Bhashyakara, explains it thus:** "riśa" is harm done in enmity, and "dasyanti" means they destroy; or they destroy the harmers; or they hurl away those who harm — such are "**riśādasaḥ**"; some say that they eat or consume the harmful, some that they hurl them away. Devarājayajvan, in his commentary on the Nighaṇṭu (4-3-53), says the root *riś* is used in the sense of harming. Commenting on the word "riśādasaḥ" in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (33-72), where it is addressed to the deities Vāyu and Savitṛ, Mahīdhara explains it as "destroyers of enemies."

old: **"Ṛtena"** — we have already fully discussed this word (see page 647). **"Ṛtāvṛdhau"** — the Bhashyakara states that "ṛta" here means "water," or, alternatively, "truth" or "the yajna." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna accept the sense "water"; Skandasvāmī has similarly explained it. **The Bhashyakara, accepting the sense "water," explains it accordingly.** Scholars of Vedic interpretation say that "ṛta" means "Dharma" (**Taking delight in the Sacred law**), and explain the word in this sense. In the present context, this meaning too is entirely fitting, since, in a Rik connected with Mitra-Varuṇa, some scholars accept the sense "rain" precisely because of the well-known connection between rain and Mitra-Varuṇa. **Others who hold that this is not the fitting sense here explain the word differently.** Various writers explain this word using three distinct meanings: **"satyam" (truth), "yajña" (the sacrifice), and "udaka" (water)**. The Bhashyakara has himself made use of all three senses across various contexts.
new: **"Ṛtena"** — we have already discussed this word (see page 647). **"Ṛtāvṛdhau"** — Yāska has explained "ṛta" as "water" (Nirukta 2-25) and as "truth" or "yajña" (Nirukta 4-19). The Bhashyakara has accepted the sense "water" and explained accordingly. The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain "ṛta" as "dharma" (**Taking delight in the Sacred law**). Although this sense is fitting for the word, in the present context and in many Riks concerning Mitra-Varuṇa they are shown as the cause of rain, as those who bring about rain; hence the sense "water" is the fitting one here for the word "ṛta." Māthava has explained it as "increasers of truth." Skandasvāmī has explained it in all three senses, yajña, water and truth. A doubt arises about the Bhashyakara's sense "water": this Rik has the two words "ṛtāvṛdhau" and "ṛtaspṛśā," and when "ṛta" is taken as water there is no reason for two words with the same meaning to stand side by side in one mantra.

old: **In the present passage, the word "vṛdhau" is used in the sense of augmenting; the word "spṛśau" (in "ṛtaspṛśā") appears twice** — [used once each] with two distinct senses. **Since it would otherwise be redundant to repeat the same word "ṛtavṛdhau" and "ṛtaspṛśā" with an identical sense, several scholars hold that "ṛtāvṛdhau" means "increasers of truth or of the yajna," while "ṛtaspṛśā," within the same word, means "bringers of water"** — this being why the [same-looking] word carries different meanings in each place. **Some scholars, however, are of the view that "ṛta" applies with only the general sense of "truth" throughout, without needing this distinction.**
new: **Therefore many scholars hold that "ṛta" in the word "ṛtāvṛdhau" means "truth" or "yajña," and that "ṛta" in the word "ṛtaspṛśā" means "water."** Where "ṛta" is given the sense "truth," that sense is generally fitting, but "ṛta" does not denote truth alone: it denotes the Universal law (dharma) by which the moving and unmoving world and the laws of creation proceed.
basis: Kannada: ritavridhau = satya/yajna, ritaspricha = udaka; rita = Universal law, not truth alone; English has an unrelated discussion of vrdhau/sprsau appearing twice

old: **Many hold that the sense "truth" fits best here.** In the context where Mitra-Varuṇa are being praised, since only the sense "truth" fits the reference clearly, it is regarded as the more suitable reading — while the fittingness of the sense "water" does not appear so clear in the other place. **"Yugas satyaṃ paraṃ brahma"** — the topic of universal righteousness and eternal order — is discussed further in the Taittiriya Upanishad (1-1-1[?]); this subject matter is treated more fully when that context is explained.
new: In Rik 10-190-1 "ṛta" and "satya" stand as two separate words, so it is clear that "ṛta" is a thing different from truth. A sentence of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (4-23-1) also supports this. The word "ṛta" will be explained more fully in another context.

Given this, "urukṣaya" is taken to mean: those who possess a settled, established dwelling — a settlement across the extended earth.
new: **"Urukṣayā"** — the Bhashyakara has explained this as "refuge of many." But since in the Rigveda "uru" (extensive) and "kṣaya" (dwelling-place) are the common senses, here "urukṣayā" is better taken as "having an extensive dwelling-place" (spread over the earth, the sky and heaven).

old: **"Dakṣaṃ"** — this word, meaning "strength," is well known from the discussion given at the very outset of this sukta (see page 699 above). The Bhashyakara here explains "dakṣa" as meaning "the power/strength of the mind." Later, however, some interpret "dakṣa" as meaning "efficiency" ("**Intellectual faculty or power; efficiency in work both mental and physical**"). Others take "dakṣa" and "buddhi-śakti" (intellectual capacity) to carry the same sense; that, too, is fitting here.
new: **"Dakṣaṃ"** — since "dakṣa" is read among the twenty-eight words meaning "strength," the Bhashyakara has explained this word as "strength." But as we have said before (see page 699), the sense given by Mahīdhara, "intellectual faculty or power; efficiency in work both mental and physical," that is, "intellectual power," is the apt one here.

old: **"Apasam"** — the Bhashyakara explains "apas" as meaning "karma" (action, rite). Further, some hold that "dakṣa" and "apas" together mean "one's own strength" and "the specific capability to accomplish the intended work." **But the fitting sense here is that "dakṣam" refers to strength itself, while "apasam" refers to that which is accomplished — the rite (the yajna).** This grants a sense to which the desire "may my rite prosper" is naturally connected.
new: **"Apasam"** — since "apas" is read among the twenty-six names of "karma," the Bhashyakara has explained "apasam" as "action (the rite)." And he has taken the two words "dakṣaṃ" and "apasaṃ" as independent nouns and explained accordingly. But if "dakṣaṃ" is made the noun and "apasaṃ" its adjective, the meaning is: "May they give us proficiency in the rites, the yajnas and the like, that we perform." This sense seems the acceptable one.
